source.title: The History of the Peloponnesian War
source.attribution: Thucydides, The History of the Peloponnesian War (trans. Richard Crawley), Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Start recording a big event while it is still happening
cards.body:
Thucydides was an Athenian who began writing the history of the war between Athens and Sparta in 431 BC, the year it broke out in Greece. He did not wait for the dust to settle. He judged early that this would be the greatest war the Greek world had known, and he took notes as events unfolded.

The war lasted 27 years, and his record is one of the main reasons we know anything about it. The habit works on a small scale too. When you sense that something important is starting in your life, a new job, an illness, a move, write things down as they happen. Memory rewrites the past quickly; notes made at the time do not.
cards.quote: Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, beginning at the moment that it broke out, and believing that it would be a great war and more worthy of relation than any that had preceded it.
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing that is changing in your life right now and write three dated lines about it tonight.

quiz.question: When did Thucydides start writing his history?
options: At the moment the war broke out
quiz.explanation: He began as soon as the war started, because he expected it to be the greatest war yet.

cards.title: Test every report, even your own memory, before you trust it
cards.body:
Thucydides refused to take his story from the first source that came to hand. He compared eyewitnesses and found that their accounts often clashed, sometimes from poor memory and sometimes because people favoured one side. He even refused to trust his own impressions without checking them.

He noticed that most people accept stories, even about their own city, without testing them at all. That is still true of news, office gossip and family legends. Before you repeat something important, ask who actually saw it, whether two independent people agree, and whether the teller has a reason to lean one way.
cards.quote: I did not even trust my own impressions, but it rests partly on what I saw myself, partly on what others saw for me, the accuracy of the report being always tried by the most severe and detailed tests possible.
cards.apply_it: Before you share the next striking claim you read, find one independent source that confirms it.

quiz.question: Why did eyewitness accounts often disagree, according to Thucydides?
options: Imperfect memory and partiality for one side
The war moved too fast to see
quiz.explanation: He blamed imperfect memory and undue partiality for one side, so he tested each report carefully.

cards.title: Make work that lasts rather than work that wins applause
cards.body:
Thucydides admitted his history would feel dry. He left out the romantic tales that made other writers popular. His aim was not to please an audience for an afternoon but to give future readers an exact picture of the past, because he believed human affairs would keep repeating in similar patterns.

He called his book a possession for all time, and 2,400 years later leaders and students still read it. The choice he faced is common: polish something for quick praise, or do the slower, plainer work that will still be useful later. When the two pull apart, ask which one you will be glad of in ten years.
cards.quote: In fine, I have written my work, not as an essay which is to win the applause of the moment, but as a possession for all time.
cards.apply_it: Name one piece of work this week where you will choose accuracy and usefulness over looking impressive.

quiz.question: What did Thucydides hope his history would be?
quiz.explanation: He wrote not for the applause of the moment but as a possession for all time, useful for understanding the future.

cards.title: Themistocles: quick judgment in a crisis can be trained by experience
cards.body:
Before the great war, Themistocles had steered Athens through the Persian invasion of 480 BC and urged it to become a sea power. Thucydides describes his extraordinary gift: in sudden crises, with no time to think, he judged best, and he could foresee where events were heading.

Yet the same Athens later exiled him, and he ended his life in Persian service, governing a town in what is now western Turkey. Thucydides reports that his bones were secretly brought home. His story shows both the value of sharp judgment under pressure and how quickly a city can turn on the person who saved it. Good instincts grow from paying close attention to how situations unfold.
cards.quote: By his own native capacity, alike unformed and unsupplemented by study, he was at once the best judge in those sudden crises which admit of little or of no deliberation, and the best prophet of the future, even to its most distant possibilities.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent surprise at work or home. Write down what you would do faster and better if it happened again.

quiz.question: What gift did Thucydides most admire in Themistocles?
options: His judgment in sudden crises and foresight
quiz.explanation: Thucydides praised his ability to judge well in emergencies and to foresee the future.

cards.title: Look past the stated reasons to the fear underneath a conflict
cards.body:
Before the war began in 431 BC, Athens and Sparta traded complaints about quarrels over Corcyra (modern Corfu) and Potidaea in northern Greece. Thucydides records them carefully. But he says the real cause was the one people spoke of least: Athens had grown powerful, and Sparta was afraid.

This idea is so famous that modern writers name rising-power rivalries after him. It applies to smaller conflicts too. Arguments at work or at home often fight over surface issues while the real driver is a fear of losing ground. Naming that fear, gently and out loud, can be more useful than winning the surface argument.
cards.quote: The growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm which this inspired in Lacedaemon, made war inevitable.
cards.apply_it: In a current disagreement, ask yourself: what is each side quietly afraid of losing?

quiz.question: What did Thucydides consider the real cause of the war?
options: Sparta's fear of Athens's growing power
quiz.explanation: He said the truest cause, least openly discussed, was Athens's rising power and the alarm it caused in Sparta.

cards.title: Restless boldness and careful caution each have a price
cards.body:
In 432 BC, at an assembly in Sparta, envoys from Corinth tried to shake the Spartans out of their caution. They described the Athenians as quick, inventive and always on the move, never content with what they had. The Spartans, they said, were good at keeping what they had but slow to act.

The Corinthians meant it as a warning, but the portrait cuts both ways. Constant drive builds empires and exhausts people; steady caution keeps things safe and can miss the moment. Most of us lean towards one style. Knowing which one is yours helps you see when to borrow a little of the other.
cards.quote: To describe their character in a word, one might truly say that they were born into the world to take no rest themselves and to give none to others.
cards.apply_it: Ask someone who knows you well: am I more restless or more cautious? Pick one decision this week to make the other way.

quiz.question: How did the Corinthians describe the Athenians?
options: Restless people who took no rest and gave none to others
quiz.explanation: They said the Athenians were born to take no rest themselves and give none to others, unlike the cautious Spartans.

cards.title: Three motives drive most power struggles: fear, honour and interest
cards.body:
At the same assembly in Sparta in 432 BC, some Athenian envoys explained frankly why Athens kept its empire. It had been offered to them after the Persian wars, they said, and they held on to it out of three strong motives: fear of what would happen if they let go, honour, and self-interest.

That simple triad is still a useful lens. When a person or organisation clings to a position, ask which of the three is at work. Fear needs reassurance, honour needs a way to save face, and interest needs a better deal. Treating all three as the same thing usually fails.
cards.quote: refused to give it up under the pressure of three of the strongest motives, fear, honour, and interest.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who won't budge on an issue. Which is it mainly: fear, honour or interest? Adjust your approach to fit.

quiz.question: Which three motives did the Athenian envoys name?
quiz.explanation: They said fear, honour and interest made them keep their empire.

cards.title: Talk it through before you act, not after the damage is done
cards.body:
The Athenian envoys at Sparta in 432 BC urged the Spartans to think hard before starting a war. Once a war is underway, they warned, it becomes a game of chance that neither side controls. They offered to settle the dispute by arbitration, as the existing treaty required.

Their sharpest line describes a mistake people still make: acting first and only discussing it once things go wrong. Big decisions deserve the hard conversation at the start, when every option is still open. Sparta voted for war anyway, and the fighting lasted 27 years.
cards.quote: It is a common mistake in going to war to begin at the wrong end, to act first, and wait for disaster to discuss the matter.
cards.apply_it: Before your next major decision, list what could go wrong and talk it over with one person before committing.

quiz.question: What common mistake did the Athenian envoys describe?
options: Acting first and discussing only after disaster
quiz.explanation: They warned against beginning at the wrong end: acting first and waiting for disaster to discuss it.

cards.title: King Archidamus warned that wars started lightly are handed to our children
cards.body:
Archidamus, king of Sparta, spoke against rushing into war in 432 BC. He had seen many wars and knew how young men long for war because they have never experienced it. Athens, he pointed out, had a navy, money and allies across the sea. Raiding Athenian farmland would not end it quickly.

He advised building strength and negotiating first. His fear that the war would outlast its makers came true: it ran for 27 years. The lesson reaches beyond war. Projects, feuds and debts begun in a rush often outlive the people who started them. Ask who will be left carrying it.
cards.quote: I fear rather that we may leave it as a legacy to our children; so improbable is it that the Athenian spirit will be the slave of their land, or Athenian experience be cowed by war.
cards.apply_it: Before starting something big, ask: if this takes ten times longer than I expect, who will be carrying it?

quiz.question: What did King Archidamus fear about the coming war?
options: It might be left as a legacy to their children
quiz.explanation: He feared the war would drag on so long that it would pass to the next generation.

cards.title: Fear your own blunders more than your rival's schemes
cards.body:
Pericles was the leading statesman of Athens when war with Sparta approached in 432 BC. In his speech urging Athens to stand firm, he set out a careful plan: rely on the navy, avoid big land battles, and do not try to win new territory during the war.

Then he added a striking line. What worried him most was not the enemy, but Athens's own errors. Thucydides later shows this was exactly how Athens lost: by ignoring his advice and overreaching. In business and life, rivals rarely sink us. Our own impatience, overconfidence and side ventures do.
cards.quote: indeed, I am more afraid of our own blunders than of the enemy’s devices.
cards.apply_it: List the three mistakes you are most likely to make on your current project, and one guard against each.

quiz.question: What did Pericles say he feared more than the enemy's plans?
quiz.explanation: He said he was more afraid of Athens's own mistakes than of the enemy's devices.

cards.title: Pericles gave away his own estate to remove any hint of favouritism
cards.body:
In 431 BC the Spartan army under King Archidamus was about to invade Attica, the countryside around Athens. Archidamus was a personal friend of Pericles. Pericles realised the Spartans might spare his farms, either out of friendship or to make Athenians suspect him of a secret deal.

So he announced in advance that if his lands were left untouched, he would hand them over to the public. Good leaders spot a conflict of interest before others do and deal with it openly. Declaring it early costs a little; being suspected later can cost everything.
cards.quote: this friendship should not extend to the detriment of the state
cards.apply_it: Is there a relationship or interest that could make your judgment look biased? Mention it openly to the people affected.

quiz.question: Why did Pericles offer his estates to the public?
options: So no one could suspect him if the Spartans spared them
quiz.explanation: He feared Archidamus might spare his lands and make Athenians suspect him, so he removed the suspicion in advance.

cards.title: Don't hold the big debate while everyone is angry
cards.body:
In 431 BC the Spartans ravaged the farms around Athens while the Athenians sheltered behind their walls. Watching their land burn, many citizens, especially the young, were furious and wanted to march out and fight a stronger army. They blamed Pericles for holding them back.

Pericles refused to call an assembly. He judged that a debate driven by rage would produce a disastrous decision, so he waited while he defended the city. Timing matters in any group. When feelings are at their peak, a vote or confrontation tends to lock in the worst choice. Let the heat drop first.
cards.quote: fearing the fatal results of a debate inspired by passion and not by prudence.
cards.apply_it: Next time a group discussion turns heated, suggest a pause and a set time to decide once things are calmer.

quiz.question: Why did Pericles avoid calling an assembly during the first invasion?
options: He feared a debate driven by passion rather than prudence
The law forbade it in wartime
He had already been removed from office
quiz.explanation: He saw anger was running high and feared the fatal results of deciding in that mood.

cards.title: We accept praise of others only up to the point we can imagine matching it
cards.body:
In the winter of 431 to 430 BC, Athens held a public funeral for its first war dead, and Pericles gave the speech. He began by admitting how hard such praise is. Friends of the dead feel it is never enough; strangers suspect exaggeration.

His explanation is sharp. People can enjoy hearing others praised only while they believe they could do as well. Beyond that point, envy creeps in, and envy turns into disbelief. Keep this in mind when you praise someone in front of their peers: specific, believable praise lands better than grand claims.
cards.quote: For men can endure to hear others praised only so long as they can severally persuade themselves of their own ability to equal the actions recounted: when this point is passed, envy comes in and with it incredulity.
cards.apply_it: When you next praise someone publicly, name one concrete thing they did rather than a sweeping compliment.

quiz.question: According to Pericles, what happens when praise of others goes beyond what listeners think they could do?
options: Envy comes in, and with it disbelief
They stop listening out of boredom
They ask for the same honours
quiz.explanation: He said envy enters, and with it incredulity, once praise passes what listeners believe they could match.

cards.title: Pericles' ideal: advancement by ability, not by class or wealth
cards.body:
In his Funeral Oration, Pericles described what he believed made Athens special. Its government, he said, served the many rather than the few. Public positions went to people for their ability, and being poor or obscure did not stop a capable person from serving.

Athens did not fully live up to this. Women, enslaved people and foreigners had no vote, and Athens ruled other cities by force. Still, the ideal of judging people by what they can do, not where they come from, has shaped democracies ever since. It is worth asking how far your own workplace or community actually practises it.
cards.quote: nor again does poverty bar the way, if a man is able to serve the state, he is not hindered by the obscurity of his condition.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone overlooked around you because of background, not ability. Find one way to give them a chance to contribute.

quiz.question: What did Pericles claim decided who rose in Athenian public life?
quiz.explanation: He claimed advancement went by capacity, and poverty did not bar a capable person.

cards.title: Discussion is not a delay; it is how wise action begins
cards.body:
Pericles praised his fellow citizens for a habit that many organisations still struggle with. Athenians, he said, did not treat discussion as an obstacle to getting things done. They saw it as the necessary first step to acting wisely. Even citizens busy with their own trades were expected to judge public matters.

He also noted that people usually decide boldly out of ignorance and hesitate once they reflect; Athens, he claimed, managed to combine daring with deliberation. In meetings today the urge to skip debate and just act is strong. Done well, a short, honest discussion saves far more time than it costs.
cards.quote: instead of looking on discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action, we think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all.
cards.apply_it: Before your next team decision, give everyone a few minutes to raise objections before you commit.

quiz.question: How did Pericles say Athenians viewed discussion?
options: As the indispensable first step to wise action
quiz.explanation: He said they treated discussion as an indispensable preliminary to wise action, not a stumbling block.

cards.title: Grief hurts most for what we were used to having
cards.body:
Near the end of his Funeral Oration, Pericles turned to the parents of the fallen. He offered them the comfort of their sons' honour, but he admitted it was a hard thing to hear. They would see in other homes the blessings they had once had themselves.

He named something true about loss: we miss most keenly what was part of our everyday life. That is why ordinary moments, an empty chair, a familiar voice absent, can hurt more than big occasions. If you are comforting someone, acknowledging those small daily absences often means more than any grand words of consolation.
cards.quote: for grief is felt not so much for the want of what we have never known, as for the loss of that to which we have been long accustomed.
cards.apply_it: If someone you know is grieving, ask about the everyday things they miss, and simply listen.

quiz.question: What did Pericles say makes grief so sharp?
options: Losing what we were long accustomed to
quiz.explanation: He said grief is felt most for the loss of what we were long used to, not for what we never knew.

cards.title: Thucydides survived the plague and recorded it so others might recognise it
cards.body:
In the summer of 430 BC, while Spartan troops ravaged the land, a terrible epidemic struck Athens. It began in the port of Piraeus and spread into the crowded city. Thucydides reports that doctors, not knowing how to treat it, died in great numbers because they were closest to the sick, and prayers and oracles did no good.

He caught the disease himself and recovered. Rather than guess at its causes, he chose to describe its symptoms carefully so that others could recognise it if it ever returned. Clear, honest records of what actually happened remain one of the most useful things anyone can leave behind after a crisis.
cards.quote: I shall simply set down its nature, and explain the symptoms by which perhaps it may be recognized by the student, if it should ever break out again.
cards.apply_it: If you've been through an illness or crisis, write down plainly what helped and what didn't, for someone who may face it next.

quiz.question: Why did Thucydides describe the plague's symptoms in detail?
options: So it could be recognised if it broke out again
quiz.explanation: He left the causes to others and recorded symptoms so it might be recognised if it returned.

cards.title: In the plague, despair and caring for the sick both cost many lives
cards.body:
Thucydides says the most terrible part of the plague was the hopelessness that seized people as soon as they felt ill. He observed that despair seemed to take away their power to resist. Meanwhile the disease spread through nursing, and those who bravely cared for friends often died themselves. Those who stayed away left the sick to die alone.

Modern medicine knows far more about infection than Athens did. But the dilemma he describes is familiar from every epidemic: caregivers carry real risk, and fear and isolation take their own toll. Protecting carers and keeping hope alive are both part of getting through.
cards.quote: By far the most terrible feature in the malady was the dejection which ensued when any one felt himself sickening, for the despair into which they instantly fell took away their power of resistance
cards.apply_it: Check in on someone who is caring for a sick relative. Ask what would make their load lighter this week.

quiz.question: What did Thucydides call the most terrible feature of the plague?
options: The dejection that set in when people felt themselves falling ill
quiz.explanation: He said the despair that came on with the first symptoms was worst, as it weakened people's resistance.

cards.title: Those who have suffered and recovered often become the kindest helpers
cards.body:
During the plague of Athens, Thucydides noticed who showed the sick the most compassion: people who had already had the disease and recovered. They knew from experience what the sufferers were going through, and since no one seemed to catch it fatally twice, they no longer feared for themselves.

The pattern holds in many kinds of hardship. People who have come through illness, grief or addiction often become the most understanding supporters of those still in it. If you have survived something hard, your experience may be exactly what someone else needs. And if you are struggling, look for those who have been there.
cards.quote: Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the dying found most compassion.
cards.apply_it: Think of a hardship you've come through. Is there someone facing it now whom you could quietly encourage?

quiz.question: Who showed the sick the most compassion during the plague?
options: Those who had recovered from the disease
quiz.explanation: Survivors knew the suffering from experience and no longer feared for themselves.

cards.title: When the future feels uncertain, people stop investing in it
cards.body:
Thucydides describes how the plague eroded ordinary restraint in Athens. Seeing the rich die suddenly and the poor inherit, people decided to spend quickly and enjoy themselves. No one wanted to work patiently towards an honourable goal when they might not live to reach it, and fear of the gods or the law faded.

This is a recognisable human reaction to deep uncertainty. When the future looks unreliable, we drift towards quick pleasures and short-term choices. Noticing that pull is the first step to resisting it. Even in hard times, small long-term commitments can keep life anchored.
cards.quote: So they resolved to spend quickly and enjoy themselves, regarding their lives and riches as alike things of a day.
cards.apply_it: When life feels uncertain, keep one small long-term habit going, like saving a little or learning a little each day.

quiz.question: How did many Athenians respond to the plague's sudden deaths?
options: They spent quickly and enjoyed themselves as if life were a day
quiz.explanation: With life so uncertain, they treated lives and riches as things of a day and chased quick pleasure.

cards.title: Pericles to an angry city: I have not changed, you have
cards.body:
By 430 BC Athens had suffered two invasions and the plague, and the people turned on Pericles. They had voted for his war policy, but now they blamed him and even sent envoys to seek peace from Sparta, without success.

Pericles called an assembly to steady them. He reminded them that he had given the same advice all along; what had changed was their mood under suffering. The Athenians fined him, yet soon elected him general again. Holding steady when opinion swings against you is hard. The test is whether your reasons have changed, or only the feelings around you.
cards.quote: I am the same man and do not alter, it is you who change, since in fact you took my advice while unhurt, and waited for misfortune to repent of it
cards.apply_it: When criticism hits, write down whether the facts have changed or only the mood, before deciding to change course.

quiz.question: What did the Athenians do to Pericles after his speech?
options: Fined him, then soon elected him general again
quiz.explanation: They fined him, but before long re-elected him general, seeing he was the best man for the crisis.

cards.title: A leader who never bought power never has to flatter
cards.body:
Pericles died in 429 BC, about two and a half years into the war. Thucydides sums up why he could lead Athens so well. Because of his rank, ability and known honesty, he could lead the people instead of being led by them. He had never gained power by improper means, so he never needed to flatter anyone, and he could even afford to anger them.

When the crowd grew overconfident he brought them down to earth; when they panicked he restored their nerve. That freedom to tell hard truths came from integrity built up over years. Leaders who owe their position to pleasing people tend to keep pleasing them, even when it does harm.
cards.quote: to lead them instead of being led by them; for as he never sought power by improper means, he was never compelled to flatter them
cards.apply_it: Is there a hard truth you've been softening to stay liked? Find a respectful way to say it plainly this week.

quiz.question: Why could Pericles afford to contradict the Athenians?
options: He never sought power by improper means, so he never needed to flatter them
quiz.explanation: His integrity meant he owed no one flattery, so he could lead rather than follow the crowd.

cards.title: The Plataeans escaped a siege by counting bricks many times over
cards.body:
Plataea was a small town in Boeotia, central Greece, allied to Athens and besieged by Sparta and Thebes from 429 BC. By the winter of 428 to 427 BC its food was running out. About 220 defenders decided to break out over the enemy's double wall.

They needed ladders of the right height, so many men counted the layers of bricks in the wall at once, again and again. A few miscounted, but most got it right, and the common answer gave the length. The breakout largely succeeded. Repeating a measurement and pooling many careful estimates is still one of the best ways to beat individual error.
cards.quote: These were counted by many persons at once; and though some might miss the right calculation, most would hit upon it, particularly as they counted over and over again
cards.apply_it: For your next important estimate, ask two or three people to work it out separately, then compare answers.

quiz.question: How did the Plataeans work out how long their ladders should be?
options: Many men counted the brick layers repeatedly and used the common answer
quiz.explanation: Many counted the bricks over and over; individual errors were outweighed by the majority getting it right.

cards.title: Decisions made in fury often look different the next morning
cards.body:
In 427 BC Mytilene, the main city of the island of Lesbos off the coast of modern Turkey, revolted against Athens and was crushed. In the heat of anger the Athenian assembly voted to kill all the men of Mytilene and enslave the women and children, and sent a ship with the order.

The next day many Athenians felt horror at punishing a whole city for the acts of the guilty, and the question was reopened. Thucydides shows that second thoughts can save lives. When you have decided something in anger, give yourself permission to look again once you have slept on it.
cards.quote: The morrow brought repentance with it and reflection on the horrid cruelty of a decree, which condemned a whole city to the fate merited only by the guilty.
cards.apply_it: If you made a harsh decision while angry recently, revisit it today with a calmer head.

quiz.question: What happened the day after Athens voted to destroy Mytilene?
options: Many regretted the cruelty and the question was reopened
quiz.explanation: The next day brought repentance, and the assembly met again to reconsider.

cards.title: Haste and passion are the two great enemies of good advice
cards.body:
At the second debate on Mytilene in 427 BC, a fierce popular leader named Cleon argued that changing their minds made Athens weak. A speaker named Diodotus answered him. He defended reopening the question and named the two things most opposed to good counsel: haste and passion.

He added that a good citizen should win by better argument, not by frightening opponents with accusations of bribery. Both points hold up. A decision is rarely improved by being rushed, and a debate is never improved by attacking people's motives instead of their reasons.
cards.quote: I think the two things most opposed to good counsel are haste and passion; haste usually goes hand in hand with folly, passion with coarseness and narrowness of mind.
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, respond to the other person's reasons rather than guessing at their motives.

quiz.question: Which two things did Diodotus call most opposed to good counsel?
quiz.explanation: He said haste goes with folly and passion with narrowness of mind.

cards.title: Harsher punishment rarely stops people driven by hope
cards.body:
Diodotus made a practical argument against killing the people of Mytilene. Cities had made death the penalty for many crimes, yet people still committed them. Hope and desire, he said, always convince people they will succeed. A city that knows surrender means death will simply fight to the last.

And the ordinary people of Mytilene had surrendered the town themselves. Killing them would turn friendly common people everywhere against Athens. Prevention through good management, he argued, works better than terror. The idea still matters in schools, workplaces and justice: fear alone rarely changes behaviour, and harsh punishment can backfire.
cards.quote: we must make up our minds to look for our protection not to legal terrors but to careful administration.
cards.apply_it: Think of a rule you enforce at home or work. Could better prevention do more than a stiffer penalty?

quiz.question: What was Diodotus's main argument against executing the Mytilenians?
options: Severe punishment does not deter and would make future rebels fight to the end
quiz.explanation: He argued terror fails to deter people driven by hope and would make enemies of potential friends.

cards.title: The second ship that arrived just in time to stop a massacre
cards.body:
Diodotus's motion won by a narrow vote, but the first ship carrying the death order had a day and a night's start. A second ship raced after it. The Mytilenian envoys promised the rowers rewards; they ate barley cakes soaked in oil and wine while rowing and slept in shifts.

The first ship, on its grim errand, went slowly. The second arrived just as the Athenian general Paches had read the decree, and stopped the massacre. Even so, more than a thousand men judged to be leaders of the revolt were executed on Cleon's motion. Mercy that comes late can still save many, so it is never too late to try to undo harm.
cards.quote: Paches had only just had time to read the decree, and to prepare to execute the sentence, when the second put into port and prevented the massacre.
cards.apply_it: If you've set something unkind in motion, act today to soften or stop it rather than assuming it's too late.

quiz.question: Why did the second ship reach Mytilene in time?
options: Its crew rowed in shifts and the first ship sailed slowly on its grim errand
quiz.explanation: The rowers worked in shifts with food at the oar, while the first ship made no haste on its horrid errand.

cards.title: Plataea's trial asked one question, and the answer was already decided
cards.body:
In the summer of 427 BC, starving Plataea surrendered to Sparta on the promise that only the guilty would be punished, and by law. Five Spartan judges arrived. They made no charge. They simply asked each prisoner whether he had done Sparta and its allies any service in the war.

The Plataeans had been loyal allies of Athens, so the answer was always no. About two hundred Plataeans and twenty-five Athenians were killed, the women enslaved, and the town later razed. Thucydides says Sparta acted mainly to please Thebes. A trial whose question guarantees the verdict is not justice, however formal it looks.
cards.quote: they simply called up the Plataeans, and asked them whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and allies any service in the war then raging.
cards.apply_it: When you judge someone, ask yourself whether your question allows any answer that could clear them.

quiz.question: What single question did the Spartan judges ask each Plataean?
options: Whether he had broken the treaty
Whether he worshipped the Spartan gods
Whether he had done Sparta and its allies any service in the war
quiz.explanation: Since Plataea had sided with Athens, the answer was always no, and the prisoners were executed.

cards.title: In civil strife, words change meaning to justify extremes
cards.body:
In 427 BC civil war broke out on Corcyra, today's Corfu. Democrats backed by Athens and oligarchs backed by Corinth and Sparta slaughtered each other, and the violence spread across Greece. Thucydides noticed something chilling: language itself was bent. Recklessness was called loyal courage; caution was called cowardice; moderation became weakness.

The extremist was trusted and anyone urging calm was suspected. This is one of the most quoted passages in political writing, because it happens again and again. When you notice everyday virtues like patience or fairness being mocked as betrayal, it is a warning sign that a group is sliding towards something dangerous.
cards.quote: Words had to change their ordinary meaning and to take that which was now given them. Reckless audacity came to be considered the courage of a loyal ally; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice
cards.apply_it: Notice one word your group now uses as an insult that used to mean something good, like 'moderate'. Say it plainly in its old sense.

quiz.question: During the Corcyraean civil war, what was 'prudent hesitation' called?
quiz.explanation: Thucydides shows how caution was renamed cowardice as words were twisted to fit party passions.

cards.title: When factions go to war, the moderates in the middle suffer first
cards.body:
Thucydides traced the cruelty at Corcyra to greed and ambition for power, dressed up in fine slogans. One side claimed to stand for the equality of the people, the other for a moderate aristocracy, but leaders on both sides used those ideals to seize advantage. Oaths of reconciliation meant nothing, and trust collapsed.

The citizens caught in between were destroyed, either because they refused to take a side or because others resented that they might escape. In any polarised group, those who try to stay fair become targets for both camps. Protecting the middle ground takes courage and support from others.
cards.quote: Meanwhile the moderate part of the citizens perished between the two, either for not joining in the quarrel, or because envy would not suffer them to escape.
cards.apply_it: If someone in your circle is trying to stay fair in a bitter dispute, tell them you value it.

quiz.question: What happened to the moderate citizens in the civil strife?
options: They fled to Sparta and prospered
They perished between the two factions
quiz.explanation: They were destroyed for not joining in, or because envy would not let them escape.

cards.title: Sparta's envoys warned Athens not to trust a lucky streak
cards.body:
In 425 BC Athenian forces trapped about 420 Spartan soldiers on Sphacteria, a small island at Pylos in the south-west of the Peloponnese. Proud Sparta sent envoys to Athens to ask for peace. They spoke frankly: people who gain unexpected good fortune tend to grasp for more, while those who have seen both good and bad times trust prosperity least.

Athens, urged on by Cleon, demanded more and refused. Thucydides later says Athens kept grasping and sent envoy after envoy away. A run of luck is the most dangerous time to raise your demands. The wise treat gains as fragile and lock in a fair outcome while they can.
cards.quote: Indeed sensible men are prudent enough to treat their gains as precarious, just as they would also keep a clear head in adversity
cards.apply_it: If things are going unusually well right now, decide one gain to secure before you push for more.

quiz.question: What did the Spartan envoys warn the Athenians about in 425 BC?
options: Grasping for more after unexpected good fortune
quiz.explanation: They urged Athens to treat its gains as precarious and make peace instead of reaching for more.

cards.title: Lasting peace comes from generosity in victory, not humiliation
cards.body:
The Spartan envoys at Athens in 425 BC also offered a deeper idea. Great feuds, they said, are rarely ended by revenge or by forcing a rival into a humiliating treaty. They end when the stronger side holds back and offers better terms than the other expected.

Then the loser owes a debt of generosity instead of a debt of revenge, and honour makes them keep the deal. People are naturally glad to give way to those who give way first. The same holds in family rifts and workplace disputes: the winner who leaves the other person their dignity gets a peace that lasts.
cards.quote: they are also by nature as glad to give way to those who first yield to them, as they are apt to be provoked by arrogance to risks condemned by their own judgment.
cards.apply_it: In a dispute you are winning, offer the other person one concession they did not expect.

quiz.question: According to the Spartan envoys, how are great enmities really settled?
options: By the stronger side choosing generosity and moderate terms
quiz.explanation: They argued generosity creates a debt of honour, while humiliation creates a debt of revenge.

cards.title: A Spartan prisoner's reply: the arrow can't tell the brave from the rest
cards.body:
After a long blockade, the Spartans on Sphacteria surrendered in 425 BC. Nearly three hundred men were taken to Athens as prisoners, about 120 of them Spartans. Nothing in the war surprised the Greeks more. Everyone had believed Spartans would die rather than lay down their arms.

Later an ally of Athens mockingly asked a prisoner whether the men who had fallen were the brave ones. He replied that an arrow would be worth a great deal if it could pick out the brave, meaning the dead were simply those the stones and arrows happened to hit. Outcomes often reflect chance more than character. Be slow to judge people by results alone.
cards.quote: the atraktos—that is, the arrow—would be worth a great deal if it could tell men of honour from the rest
cards.apply_it: Next time you judge someone by an outcome, ask how much of it was luck.

quiz.question: What did the Spartan prisoner mean with his remark about the arrow?
options: The dead were simply those the missiles happened to hit, not the bravest
quiz.explanation: He pointed out that chance, not courage, decided who fell.

cards.title: Brasidas won cities by being fair, and made Sparta look better
cards.body:
Brasidas was a Spartan commander who marched to Thrace, in what is now northern Greece, in 424 BC. Many towns there were subject allies of Athens. Thucydides says Brasidas won many of them over not only by force or secret deals, but by his just and moderate treatment of the towns.

He behaved so well that people assumed all Spartans were like him, a reputation that helped Sparta long after his death in 422 BC. One person's conduct can shape how a whole group is seen. When you represent your company, family or country, people judge everyone by you.
cards.quote: He was the first who went out and showed himself so good a man at all points as to leave behind him the conviction that the rest were like him.
cards.apply_it: Where do you represent a group to outsiders? Do one thing this week that would make them think well of everyone in it.

quiz.question: How did Brasidas win over many towns from Athens?
options: By his just and moderate conduct
quiz.explanation: Thucydides credits his fairness, which also convinced people that all Spartans were like him.

cards.title: Thucydides turned twenty years of exile into a better view of the war
cards.body:
In the winter of 424 to 423 BC, Brasidas suddenly attacked Amphipolis, an Athenian colony in northern Greece. Thucydides, then an Athenian general, was half a day's sail away on the island of Thasos. He rushed seven ships there but arrived the same evening the town surrendered, and could only save the nearby port of Eion.

Athens exiled him for twenty years. He tells this plainly, without excuses. Then he used his exile: living among both sides, especially the Peloponnesians, gave him the leisure and access to see events closely. A painful setback can open a vantage point you would never have chosen.
cards.quote: It was also my fate to be an exile from my country for twenty years after my command at Amphipolis; and being present with both parties, and more especially with the Peloponnesians by reason of my exile, I had leisure to observe affairs somewhat particularly.
cards.apply_it: Think of a setback you're living with. What can you now see or learn that you couldn't from your old position?

quiz.question: What did Thucydides gain from his exile?
options: The chance to observe both sides of the war closely
quiz.explanation: Exile let him spend time with both sides and observe events in detail.

cards.title: Ask who gains from a conflict continuing
cards.body:
In 422 BC both Cleon of Athens and Brasidas of Sparta were killed in a battle at Amphipolis. Thucydides notes that they had been the chief opponents of peace on each side. Brasidas loved the success and honour that war gave him. Cleon feared that in peacetime his crimes would be noticed and his slanders less believed.

With them gone, leaders who wanted peace came forward, and the Peace of Nicias was signed in 421 BC, though it never truly held. When a quarrel drags on, it is worth asking who benefits from keeping it alive. Sometimes the people loudest for the fight have private reasons.
cards.quote: who had been the two principal opponents of peace on either side—the latter from the success and honour which war gave him, the former because he thought that, if tranquillity were restored, his crimes would be more open to detection and his slanders less credited
cards.apply_it: In an ongoing dispute around you, ask quietly: who gains if this never ends?

quiz.question: Why, according to Thucydides, did Cleon oppose peace?
options: He feared his crimes would be exposed in peacetime
quiz.explanation: Thucydides says Cleon feared that peace would expose his crimes and weaken his slanders.

cards.title: The Melian dialogue: when power decides that justice does not count
cards.body:
In 416 BC Athens sent a force to Melos, a small island in the Aegean that wanted to stay neutral. Thucydides recreates the talks as a dialogue. The Athenian envoys refuse to discuss right and wrong. Justice, they say, matters only between equals; otherwise the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

The Melians refused to give up their freedom. After a siege the town surrendered, the Athenians killed the men and enslaved the women and children. The dialogue remains a stark lesson in how power talks when it thinks no one can stop it, and why rules that protect the weak matter to everyone.
cards.quote: right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
cards.apply_it: Where do you hold power over someone? Ask yourself how you would want to be treated in their place.

quiz.question: What did the Athenian envoys tell the Melians about justice?
options: It is only in question between equals in power
quiz.explanation: They claimed right applies only between equals, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

cards.title: Hope comforts you in danger, but it is expensive
cards.body:
The Melians held out hope that the gods or Sparta would save them. The Athenian envoys answered with a cold warning about hope. Those with plenty to spare can afford it, they said, but people who stake everything on it only see its true nature when they are ruined.

The Athenians were bullies, and their own city's hopes would later fail in Sicily. Still, the warning stands on its own. Hope is precious for keeping spirits up, but it is a poor plan. Before betting everything on a hoped-for rescue, ask what real resources and evidence you have.
cards.quote: Hope, danger’s comforter, may be indulged in by those who have abundant resources, if not without loss at all events without ruin; but its nature is to be extravagant
cards.apply_it: For one hope you're counting on, write down the concrete evidence for it and a fallback if it fails.

quiz.question: What did the Athenian envoys say about hope?
options: It can be afforded by those with resources, but is extravagant by nature
It is a gift from the gods
quiz.explanation: They warned that hope is a comfort that those staking everything see clearly only when ruined.

cards.title: Athens voted to conquer Sicily without knowing how big it was
cards.body:
In the winter of 416 to 415 BC, Athens decided to send a great fleet to Sicily. Thucydides says most Athenians had no idea of the island's size or how many people lived there, Greek and non-Greek. They were taking on a war almost as large as the one against Sparta.

They were also misled: envoys from Egesta, a Sicilian city seeking help, painted an attractive and untrue picture of the money waiting there. Big commitments made in ignorance, on the word of people who want something from you, are a recipe for disaster. Check the facts for yourself first.
cards.quote: most of them being ignorant of its size and of the number of its inhabitants, Hellenic and barbarian, and of the fact that they were undertaking a war not much inferior to that against the Peloponnesians.
cards.apply_it: Before your next big commitment, verify one key claim independently instead of relying on the person who benefits.

quiz.question: What did most Athenians not know when they voted to invade Sicily?
quiz.explanation: Thucydides says most were ignorant of Sicily's size and population, and so of the scale of the war.

cards.title: When enthusiasm takes over, doubters stay silent
cards.body:
Nicias, a cautious and respected general, opposed the Sicilian expedition in 415 BC. When argument failed, he tried exaggerating the size of the force needed, hoping to scare the Athenians off. It backfired. They decided that a bigger force made the venture safe, and grew even keener.

Thucydides writes that everyone fell in love with the enterprise, and the few who disliked it kept quiet for fear of seeming unpatriotic. That silence is how groups walk into disasters. If you lead, make dissent safe; if you doubt, say so clearly rather than hoping a clever tactic will do it for you.
cards.quote: With this enthusiasm of the majority, the few that liked it not, feared to appear unpatriotic by holding up their hands against it, and so kept quiet.
cards.apply_it: At your next group decision, invite the strongest case against the plan before agreeing.

quiz.question: How did the Athenians react to Nicias's huge estimate of the forces needed?
options: They became even more eager, thinking a large force made it safe
quiz.explanation: His tactic backfired: the bigger force made the expedition seem safe, and enthusiasm grew.

cards.title: Alcibiades: brilliant in public, distrusted in private
cards.body:
Alcibiades was a young, rich and dazzling Athenian aristocrat who championed the Sicilian expedition, hoping for glory and wealth. He had entered seven chariots at the Olympic games and won first prize. Thucydides says his lavish lifestyle outran his means, and many Athenians suspected him of wanting to make himself tyrant.

Thucydides judges that his public conduct of the war was as good as anyone could wish, yet his private habits offended so many that Athens handed affairs to others, which helped ruin the city. Talent is not enough. How you live day to day decides whether people will trust you with what you are capable of.
cards.quote: although publicly his conduct of the war was as good as could be desired, individually, his habits gave offence to every one, and caused them to commit affairs to other hands, and thus before long to ruin the city.
cards.apply_it: Is any private habit undermining the trust people place in your work? Choose one to change.

quiz.question: Why, according to Thucydides, did Athens stop trusting Alcibiades?
options: His private habits and lifestyle offended people
quiz.explanation: Though his public war leadership was excellent, his private habits caused Athens to turn to others.

cards.title: In a climate of suspicion, Athens drove away its best general
cards.body:
Just before the fleet sailed in 415 BC, the stone Hermae, sacred figures at doorways across Athens, were smashed in one night. Fear of a plot spread. Alcibiades was accused of mocking sacred rites and asked to be tried at once, but his enemies delayed the trial until he was gone.

Thucydides says Athens, in its suspicious mood, welcomed every informer without testing them and jailed good citizens on the word of rascals. A ship was sent to bring Alcibiades home for trial. He slipped away at Thurii in southern Italy, fled to the Peloponnese and was sentenced to death in his absence. Panic about plots tends to punish the innocent and create real enemies.
cards.quote: instead of testing the informers, in their suspicious temper welcomed all indifferently, arresting and imprisoning the best citizens upon the evidence of rascals
cards.apply_it: Before acting on an accusation, ask what evidence supports it and who gains from it being believed.

quiz.question: How did the Athenians handle informers after the Hermae affair?
options: They welcomed all without testing and jailed good citizens
quiz.explanation: In their suspicious mood, they believed rascals and imprisoned the best citizens.

cards.title: Beware the clever speech that turns betrayal into loyalty
cards.body:
In the winter of 415 to 414 BC, Alcibiades, now an outlaw from Athens, spoke to the Spartans. He urged them to send help to Syracuse and to fortify a base in Attica, advice that badly hurt Athens. He also had to explain why a lover of his country was helping its enemies.

His answer was to redefine patriotism: the true patriot, he said, is the one who will go to any length to win his country back. It was persuasive, and Sparta followed his plan. People who switch sides often reframe their choices in noble words. Notice when an argument conveniently makes the speaker's self-interest sound like virtue.
cards.quote: love of country is what I do not feel when I am wronged, but what I felt when secure in my rights as a citizen.
cards.apply_it: When someone's argument perfectly matches their self-interest, list what they would gain if you agreed.

quiz.question: How did Alcibiades justify helping Sparta against Athens?
options: He redefined patriotism as doing anything to recover his country
He said Sparta was in the right
quiz.explanation: He argued the true lover of his country will go to any length to win it back.

cards.title: Nicias put the bad news in writing because people prefer good news
cards.body:
By the winter of 414 to 413 BC the Athenian army at Syracuse was in trouble. A Spartan commander, Gylippus, had arrived, and the besiegers had become the besieged. Nicias feared that messengers would soften the truth to please the assembly, so he wrote a letter instead.

In it he said he could have written something more pleasant but nothing more useful. He knew the Athenians liked to hear the best side and then blame the teller when hopes failed. He asked them to recall the army or send a second one, and asked to be relieved because of a kidney illness. Writing hard news clearly protects the truth from being softened on the way.
cards.quote: Besides I know that it is your nature to love to be told the best side of things, and then to blame the teller if the expectations which he has raised in your minds are not answered by the result
cards.apply_it: If you have bad news to pass up the chain, write it down clearly and plainly rather than softening it in conversation.

quiz.question: Why did Nicias send a letter rather than rely only on messengers?
options: He wanted to keep it secret from Sparta
He feared messengers might soften the truth to please the crowd
quiz.explanation: He worried messengers might forget, misspeak or tell the crowd what it wanted, so he wrote the facts himself.

cards.title: A lunar eclipse kept the Athenians at Syracuse until it was too late
cards.body:
In the summer of 413 BC, after more defeats, the Athenian generals at Syracuse in Sicily finally prepared to sail away. Then, on the night they were ready, there was an eclipse of the moon. Most of the soldiers took it as a sign to wait.

Thucydides says Nicias was overly devoted to divination, and he refused even to discuss leaving until the 27 days prescribed by soothsayers had passed. In that time the Syracusans trapped the fleet in the harbour. A decision you have reasoned out should not be thrown away because of an omen or a passing feeling.
cards.quote: Nicias, who was somewhat over-addicted to divination and practices of that kind, refused from that moment even to take the question of departure into consideration, until they had waited the thrice nine days prescribed by the soothsayers.
cards.apply_it: Is a superstition or vague fear delaying a decision you've already reasoned through? Set a date to act.

quiz.question: What stopped the Athenians from leaving Syracuse when they were ready?
options: A Spartan blockade already in place
An eclipse of the moon, after which Nicias insisted on waiting
quiz.explanation: After a lunar eclipse, Nicias refused to discuss departure until 27 days had passed.

cards.title: Nicias lived virtuously and still met a cruel end
cards.body:
After the failed retreat in 413 BC, Nicias surrendered to the Spartan commander Gylippus, trusting that Sparta remembered his efforts for peace. Gylippus wanted to bring him to Sparta alive. But some Syracusans feared what he might reveal under torture, and the Corinthians feared he might bribe his way free, so Nicias and his fellow general Demosthenes were put to death.

Thucydides gives Nicias a moving epitaph: no Greek of his time deserved such a fate less. Good character does not guarantee a good outcome, and honest effort can still end in failure. That is a reason for compassion when we judge others, and ourselves, by how things turned out.
cards.quote: This or the like was the cause of the death of a man who, of all the Hellenes in my time, least deserved such a fate, seeing that the whole course of his life had been regulated with strict attention to virtue.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who did their honest best and still failed. Tell them their effort was seen.

quiz.question: How did Thucydides judge the death of Nicias?
options: As the fate least deserved by any Greek of his time
quiz.explanation: He wrote that of all Greeks in his time, Nicias least deserved such a fate, having lived with strict attention to virtue.

cards.title: The Sicilian disaster: few out of many returned home
cards.body:
The great Athenian expedition ended in September 413 BC. The army was cut down on its retreat, and the survivors were packed into the stone quarries of Syracuse. Thucydides describes the prisoners crowded without shelter, suffering heat by day and cold by night, with little food or water, and the dead left among the living. At least seven thousand were captured; after about seventy days most non-Athenians were sold.

He calls it the greatest event of the war: most glorious to the victors, most calamitous to the defeated. Behind grand ambitions lie ordinary people who pay the price. Count that cost honestly before any bold venture.
cards.quote: they were destroyed, as the saying is, with a total destruction, their fleet, their army, everything was destroyed, and few out of many returned home.
cards.apply_it: Before your next bold plan, write down who would bear the cost if it fails, and whether they agreed to it.

quiz.question: How did Thucydides sum up the end of the Sicilian expedition?
options: Total destruction, with few out of many returning home
quiz.explanation: Fleet, army and everything were destroyed, and few out of many came home.

cards.title: After Sicily, Athens blamed the speakers for a war it had voted for
cards.body:
When news of the Sicilian disaster reached Athens in 413 BC, people at first refused to believe it. Once they accepted it, they turned their anger on the orators who had promoted the expedition and on the soothsayers who had promised victory, as if they had not voted for it themselves.

Yet Thucydides also shows the city recovering: it resolved to fight on, built a new fleet, cut spending and appointed a board of elders to advise it. Blaming others is the easy first reaction to failure. Owning your part in a group decision is harder, and it is what makes real recovery possible.
cards.quote: they were angry with the orators who had joined in promoting the expedition, just as if they had not themselves voted it
cards.apply_it: Think of a group decision that went wrong. Name your own part in it, out loud or on paper.

quiz.question: How did the Athenians first react once they accepted the news from Sicily?
options: They blamed the orators and soothsayers, as if they had not voted for it
quiz.explanation: They were angry with those who promoted the expedition, forgetting that they had voted for it.

cards.title: Alcibiades stopped Athenians from turning their fleet on their own city
cards.body:
In 411 BC a group of oligarchs called the Four Hundred seized power in Athens. The Athenian fleet at Samos, an island off the coast of modern Turkey, stayed loyal to democracy and was furious. The sailors wanted to sail home and attack their own city, which would have handed Ionia and the Hellespont to Sparta.

Alcibiades, recently returned to the Athenian side, held them back when no one else could. Thucydides calls it his first real service to the state. Alcibiades reminded them that if the city survived, the two sides might one day reconcile; if either was destroyed, there would be no one left to reconcile with. Keep that in mind in any family or team split.
cards.quote: since if the city were saved there was good hope that the two parties might some day be reconciled
cards.apply_it: In a bitter split you're part of, choose one action that keeps the door open to reconciliation later.

quiz.question: What did Alcibiades prevent the fleet at Samos from doing in 411 BC?
options: Sailing to attack their own city of Athens
quiz.explanation: He stopped them from sailing against Athens, arguing that reconciliation was possible only if the city survived.

cards.title: Athens fell to its own divisions before its enemies
cards.body:
Thucydides' account breaks off in 411 BC, but he knew how the war ended. In 404 BC, after 27 years, Sparta took Athens and pulled down its Long Walls. Looking back, he wrote that even after Sicily, with its allies in revolt and Persia's prince Cyrus paying for Sparta's navy, Athens held out for years.

It did not finally fall, he says, until its own internal quarrels destroyed it. Strong teams, families and nations are seldom beaten from outside while they stay united. Guarding unity, through fair leadership and honest debate, is often the most important defence there is.
cards.quote: Nor did they finally succumb till they fell the victims of their own intestine disorders.
cards.apply_it: Name one division in a group you belong to, and take one step this week to mend it.

quiz.question: According to Thucydides, what finally brought Athens down?
quiz.explanation: He wrote that Athens held out long after Sicily and only fell when its own internal strife destroyed it.
